objects.name: Drive-by Compromise
objects.description: Drive-by Compromise is a way for attackers to gain access to a computer when a person visits a website during normal browsing. The site, or something it loads, delivers malicious code to the browser. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Initial Access technique.

MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1105.

objects.name: Archive Collected Data

objects.description: Archive collected data is when an attacker packs stolen files into compressed or encrypted bundles before sending them out. objects.description: System Information Discovery is when an attacker collects details about a device, such as its operating system version, patch level and hardware. The attacker uses this to decide what to do next on that device. It is a Discovery technique in MITRE ATT&CK.

MITRE ATT&CK T1574: Hijack Execution Flow

objects.description: DLL hijacking is when an attacker abuses the shared library files (DLLs) that Windows programs load. A trusted program is made to load a harmful DLL instead of, or alongside, the real one. This helps the attacker stay in place, gain higher privileges and avoid detection.

objects.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1195.002: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
MITRE ATT&CK T1195: Supply Chain Compromise

objects.description: Compromise Software Supply Chain is a way for attackers to reach many computers through software they already trust. They change an application before it gets to the user, for example in its source code, its update system or its download. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Initial Access technique.

objects.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1505.003: Server Software Component: Web Shell
MITRE ATT&CK T1505: Server Software Component

objects.description: A web shell is a small script that an attacker places on a web server. It lets the attacker run commands on that server from a distance. Because it sits on the server itself, it keeps working even if the first way in is closed, which is why attackers use it to keep access to the network over time.

objects.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1068: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

objects.description: Exploitation for privilege escalation is when an attacker uses a flaw in software to gain higher permissions than they started with. For example, they may go from a normal user account to full control of the system. The flaw can be in the operating system, in software running with higher permissions, or in a signed driver. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1068.

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1555: Credentials from Password Stores

objects.description: Credentials from password stores is when an attacker looks in the places where passwords are saved and takes the logins they find. These places include system password storage, saved browser logins, password managers and cloud secrets vaults. Stolen logins can then be used to move to other systems.

objects.name: Obfuscated Files or Information

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1027: Obfuscated Files or Information

objects.description: Obfuscated Files or Information is a technique where an attacker hides the real content of a file, program or command by encrypting, encoding or packing it. The goal is to slip past security tools and make analysis harder. Tools look for known patterns, so changing how content looks can stop the patterns matching while it still runs.

objects.name: Data from Local System

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1005: Data from Local System

objects.description: Data from local system is when an attacker searches a computer they already control to find files and other data worth taking. This usually happens before the data is sent out of the network. It can cover documents, settings files, databases and more.

objects.name: Encrypted Channel

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK TA0011: Command and Control

objects.description: Encrypted Channel is a technique where attackers encrypt the traffic they use to control a compromised system. The encryption hides what is being sent, so security tools that read network traffic see only scrambled data. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1573 under Command and Control, and lists Emotet, gh0st RAT and NETWIRE as using it.

Modify Registry
objects.description: Modify Registry is a technique where an attacker changes settings in the Windows Registry. The Registry holds configuration for the system and its software. Changes can help an attacker stay on a machine, hide data or weaken security settings. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1112 under Defense Impairment and Persistence.

objects.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1041: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

objects.description: Exfiltration over a C2 channel is when an attacker sends stolen data out through the same channel they already use to control the infected system. The data is hidden inside what looks like normal control traffic, so no second route out of the network is needed. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1041 under Exfiltration.

objects.name: Phishing

external_references.description: Cyber Threat Actors Use a Variety of Techniques to Target Election and Campaign Officials

objects.description: Phishing is when an attacker sends a message that tricks someone into opening a malicious file, following a link or giving away a password. It is a common first step into a network. Defenders check attachments and links before delivery, use multi-factor authentication and make it easy for staff to report suspicious messages.

objects.description: Masquerading is when an attacker changes how a file, program, service or account looks so it seems legitimate. They may change its name, where it sits or its descriptive details. The aim is to avoid being noticed by people and by security tools.

objects.description: Account Discovery is when an attacker builds a list of valid accounts, usernames or email addresses on a system or inside a compromised environment. Knowing which accounts exist helps them plan what to do next. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as a Discovery technique.

Scheduled Task/Job
objects.description: Scheduled Task/Job is a technique where an attacker uses the task scheduling feature built into an operating system. The feature runs a program or script at a set time or on a repeat. Attackers use it to start malicious code, to keep their access after a restart, or to run code with higher privileges.

objects.name: Input Capture
objects.description: Input capture is when an attacker records what a user types or enters, to steal passwords or other information. It can happen silently in the background or by tricking the user into typing into a fake prompt or page. MITRE lists four forms: keylogging, GUI input capture, web portal capture and credential API hooking.

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1056.001: Input Capture: Keylogging

objects.name: Application Layer Protocol
objects.description: Application Layer Protocol is a technique where attackers talk to a system they control using ordinary network protocols, such as those used for web browsing, file transfer, email or DNS. Because the traffic looks like normal traffic, it is harder to spot and block. MITRE tracks it as T1071 under the Command and Control tactic.

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1071: Application Layer Protocol
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic TA0011: Command and Control

objects.name: User Execution
objects.description: User Execution is when an attacker gets a person to run malicious code for them. The person might open a file, click a link or turn on a remote access tool without knowing the risk. It is an Execution technique in MITRE ATT&CK.

objects.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
objects.description: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is when malware checks whether it is running inside a virtual machine or an analysis sandbox, and changes what it does if it is. The aim is to avoid being studied. MITRE lists it under both Stealth and Discovery.

objects.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
objects.description: Boot or logon autostart execution is when an attacker sets up a computer so that their program starts by itself when the system boots or a user logs on. This lets the attacker stay on the system after a restart. Some of these startup items run with higher privileges, so it can also help the attacker gain more control.

external_references.description: MITRE ATT&CK T1547: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution

objects.name: Hide Artifacts
objects.description: Hide Artifacts is a technique where attackers hide the traces of their activity, such as files, folders, user accounts or running tasks. The aim is to avoid being noticed by users and security tools. Attackers abuse operating system features that already hide items, so what is hidden is harder to find during a routine check. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1564.
